title: Execs unfiltered on every AFC team's draft: Are things finally looking up for Jets, Raiders? Is it really OK to feel good about the Jets? Meanwhile, reviews were mixed on the Bills', Jaguars' and Texans' draft classes. Mike Sando 4
summary:
Fernando Mendoza (right) is officially a Raider. Meanwhile David Bailey (center) and Kadyn Proctor headed draft classes praised by many around the league. Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; Photos: Ethan Miller / Getty Images, Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
After dissecting NFC teams’ drafts Thursday , we’re back with NFL executives’ insights into how all 16 AFC teams handled the annual player selection process.
Did the Buffalo Bills make wise use of all those picks (10) after trading
full_text:
Fernando Mendoza (right) is officially a Raider. Meanwhile David Bailey (center) and Kadyn Proctor headed draft classes praised by many around the league. Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; Photos: Ethan Miller / Getty Images, Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
After dissecting NFC teams’ drafts Thursday , we’re back with NFL executives’ insights into how all 16 AFC teams handled the annual player selection process.
Did the Buffalo Bills make wise use of all those picks (10) after trading down? Was the Cleveland Browns’ draft as good as the analysts suggested? Do the Houston Texans care what anyone thinks? Should the Indianapolis Colts regret the Sauce Gardner trade? Does anyone have anything good to say about Jaguars general manager James Gladstone? Is it really OK to feel good about the New York Jets?
Execs answer these and many more questions during my annual draft review.
For each team, we’ve included where it ranked in draft capital used (calculated using an NFL analytical model) and in Dane Brugler’s favorite classes , along with how many times it traded up or down during the draft (excluding deals that involved veteran players).
Draft capital rank: 11th | Brugler’s rank: 11th | Trades up/down: 1/0
The Ravens continued their recent trend of targeting less-premium positions in the first round, inviting an interesting philosophical discussion.
Guard Olaivavega Ioane (No. 14 this year) joins safety Malaki Starks (No. 27 in 2025), safety Kyle Hamilton (No. 14 in 2022) and center Tyler Linderbaum (No. 25 in 2022) among the recent Baltimore first-rounders fitting that mold.
All qualify as solid or even spectacular players.
Execs see Ioane as a high-odds prospect as well.
“Really good, good player — probably the best guard in the draft,” one said.
A thick, nasty mauler on track to be a long-term NFL starter.
The problem, if there is one, is that teams are generally less likely to re-sign players at these positions once their rookie contracts expire (Hamilton, the lone superstar among the group, did sign a four-year, $100.4 million deal before last season).
“The positional-value talk before the draft was interesting — teams said you can throw that out this year with the premium players playing non-premium positions,” another exec said. “(Sonny) Styles, (Caleb) Downs, (Jeremiyah) Love all fit that. Guards are expensive now, so it’s not as bad to pick up their options.
“Indy made it work with Quenton Nelson, and he was picked a lot higher (No. 6) than Ioane.”
Linderbaum’s case is instructive. He was everything the Ravens could have hoped, starting 66 of a possible 68 career games, earning three consecutive Pro Bowl honors and ranking fourth in Pro Football Focus’ grading for centers last season. But Baltimore declined his fifth-year option last spring because the value ($23.4 million) is tied to all offensive linemen (not centers, specifically). When his deal expired after four years, the Raiders signed him to a three-year, $81 million deal, resetting the market at the position by roughly 50 percent.
No one faults Baltimore for failing to meet that steep price, but if Ioane leaves in four years, no one should be shocked, either.
The void at center endures for Baltimore.
After using the first-round pick on Ioane and a second-rounder on an edge rusher (Zion Young), the Ravens watched two centers come off the board — Logan Jones to Chicago at No. 57, Jake Slaughter to the Chargers at No. 63 — before they were back on the clock at No. 80 and took receiver Ja’Kobi Lane.
Garrett Bradbury, acquired by Chicago from New England this offseason, would be a logical trade target if the Bears like what they see from Jones, the center they drafted in the second round. Bradbury played at NC State when current Ravens offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford coached the position for the Wolfpack.
“Baltimore is going to let everybody who can snap the ball try,” an exec said. “That would not be a bad trade. If I’m Chicago, I would not trade him until I know what I have with Logan Jones and know he is the guy.”
The Ravens doubled up on receiver and tight end in the third through fifth rounds.
“Ja’Kobi Lane is really talented — he has ability, but he’s really inconsistent,” an exec said of the Ravens’ third-round receiver. “(Matthew) Hibner is a good route-running tight end, has a little speed, catches it well, is perfect for them to develop. But he doesn’t have the body control that (Isaiah) Likely had.”
Draft capital rank: 25th | Brugler’s rank: 22nd | Trades up/down: 1/6
Execs admired the Bills’ ability to maneuver around the board while making a league-high seven in-draft trades, but reviews were mixed regarding the players Buffalo wound up selecting.
“Those picks you gain, whether it’s a third or fourth or something later, they were not going to net you any (good) players in this draft,” one exec said.
Time will tell on that front. The team drafted 10 players, tied for third-most in the league, and used its second-rounder to acquire receiver DJ Moore from Chicago.
“I do think there’s some element of regime change with (coach) Joe Brady and (GM) Brandon (Beane) wanting to make this his team and put in his stamp on it,” another exec said. “(Having) more picks probably helps do that. But again, this was a weird draft, in that it was terrible at the top and terrible at the bottom.”
“There was no sweet spot to accumulate picks,” this exec added. “I do not really begrudge anybody’s strategy in this draft, because I don’t know what you were supposed to do to be effective.”
The Bills traded down from 26 to 28, then to 31, then to 35, where they selected Clemson edge rusher T.J. Parker.
“The issue I have is, they took guys who have questionable play style,” a third exec said. “If you asked them what their identity is, they might say tough, physical, all these things. But you look at the guys they drafted, and it’s not that.”
“I was a big fan of Parker,” a different exec said. “Real young kid. Huge upside. The problem is, those Clemson defensive linemen, they just haven’t really developed, so there’s a little bit of a concern there.”
Still learning some moves, but offers playmaking potential against both run and pass.
Draft capital rank: 28th | Brugler’s rank: 24th | Trades up/down: 0/1
Execs applauded the Bengals’ decision to trade the 10th pick to the Giants for nose tackle Dexter Lawrence. They saw it as the surest way available for the Bengals to upgrade their defense and demonstrate to quarterback Joe Burrow that the team was serious, two huge priorities this offseason.
“This is like the NBA when you are trying to acquire guys to keep your star who is going to leave happy,” one exec said. “Is it expensive? Sure, but there is no price on keeping Burrow happy. Drafting Rueben Bain does not make Burrow happy.”
The Bengals also traded down with the Jets, who selected quarterback Cade Klubnik with Cincinnati’s pick in the fourth round. That deal helped the Bengals land receiver Colbie Young along with center Connor Lew.
“Young is legit — he’s big, and he’s got good hips and really good instincts for route running,” another exec said. “He is an outside receiver, though, so there is no one who can play the slot for them unless they put Ja’Marr Chase in there. It’s a helluva value pick. I just don’t know how you play all three at once.”
After effectively landing Lawrence with the 10th pick, the Bengals addressed defense with their own second- and third-round picks. They already added Boye Mafe, Bryan Cook and Jonathan Allen to deals totaling $45.9 million in average salary after letting edge rushers Trey Hendrickson and Joseph Ossai leave in free agency.
“Dexter Lawrence would be a top-five pick in this draft even at his age,” a third exec said. “There is no one like him in this draft. He can change their defense, coupled with what they did in free agency.”

full_text:
For the third consecutive draft, the Panthers added a receiver as a potential playmaker for QB Bryce Young. Jared C. Tilton / Getty Images
CHARLOTTE, N.C. — Just as no general manager ever reveals state secrets at pre-draft news conferences, it’s also a NFL truism that general managers like to brag on themselves and the work of their scouting departments at post-draft pressers.
Such was the case last weekend with Dan Morgan.
“We felt like we definitely got better. We challenged the roster in a lot of spots, gained a lot of depth in a lot of areas,” the Panthers general manager said. “We feel good about what we accomplished during the draft and excited about things moving forward. We’re obviously headed in the right direction.”
In the Panthers’ case, industry experts agreed.
The Athletic’s Austin Mock gave the Panthers an A in his draft grades, which place a premium on teams that gained the most surplus value — a prospect’s on-field value relative to his rookie contract — among their draft picks. It’s the second year in a row the Panthers have finished in the top five in Mock’s grades.
“For picking outside of the top 10, the Panthers did a phenomenal job addressing premium positions and team needs,” Mock wrote, “while also drafting players lower than their consensus ranks.”
Pro Football Focus handed Carolina an even better grade, rating the draft class an A-plus and calling the Panthers “the offseason champions” for following up on a strong free agency.
But on a more micro level, the Panthers’ draft haul wasn’t necessarily a positive for every player or position group, which The Athletic analyzes with its annual look at the team’s winners and losers following the draft.
The Panthers brought Indiana running back Kaelon Black in for a 30 visit and had a virtual meeting with Nebraska’s Emmett Johnson. That prompted some to wonder whether Morgan might use a Day-2 or Day-3 pick on a running back as insurance for Brooks, who is attempting to come back from a second ACL surgery on his right knee. Instead, the Panthers will head into OTAs with Brooks, Etienne and free-agent acquisition AJ Dillon behind starter Chuba Hubbard. Brooks said he has been cleared by his surgeon to participate in OTAs, but indicated he’s not yet 100 percent. “The training staff has a great plan for me. I’ve been working out with Chuba,” Brooks said this week. “I’m getting there. It’s just gonna take time, but I’m getting there.”
This is the third consecutive year Young has emerged from the draft as a “winner” on this list, coinciding with Morgan’s decision to take a wide receiver for the third year in a row. It wasn’t a first-round pick this year, nor was it a yards-after-catch receiver the Panthers were believed to be looking for. Still, third-round pick Chris Brazzell gives Young and the offense something it lacked: A big vertical threat who can fly. Brazzell’s ability to come down with deep balls should mesh will Young’s touch on long throws. In addition to Brazzell, Morgan selected two offensive linemen for the first time in his three drafts, and left tackle Monroe Freeling and center Sam Hecht could be protecting Young for quite a while.
Oregon safety Dillon Thieneman was frequently linked to the Panthers by mock drafters, who viewed Thieneman’s combination of speed and ball skills as a good complement to Tre’von Moehrig’s in-the-box tenaciousness. After Morgan chose Freeling with the 19th pick, Thieneman fell to the Chicago Bears six spots later. The Panthers also passed on Toledo safety Emmanuel McNeil-Warren in the second round. By waiting until the fifth round to draft Penn State safety Zakee Wheatley, it means the Panthers will roll into OTAs with Scott atop the depth chart at free safety. Scott re-signed on a one-year, $2 million deal following a season in which he started 17 games and finished with 111 tackles, both career highs. Scott has a long history with defensive coordinator Ejiro Evero, having played for him in five of his seven seasons.
Similar to Scott’s situation, Wallace appears to have kept his starting spot as a result of Morgan waiting until Day 3 to draft an off-ball linebacker — seventh-rounder Jackson Kuwatch from Miami (Ohio). Wallace, a third-round pick in 2024, is coming off season-ending shoulder surgery in December. The former Kentucky standout ranked 85th out of 85 qualified linebackers last year with a PFF run-defense grade of 42.2. Panthers coach Dave Canales said Wallace has done “really great in terms of getting back out there” for offseason workouts. With Kuwatch expected to be a special teams player, Wallace figures to begin training camp on the first-team defense alongside Devin Lloyd.
Walker and Fortner were penciled in as starters at left tackle and center, respectively, entering the draft weekend. But given that both signed one-year, team-friendly deals, it was considered likely that Morgan would address one or both positions in the draft. That’s how it played out, with the Panthers taking Freeling in the first round and Hecht in the fifth with Morgan’s best value pick. Canales and Morgan made a point not to anoint any of the draft picks as immediate starters, and Freeling and Hecht will have to compete with the two veterans. Those figure to be a couple of the more closely watched position battles of the spring and summer.
Whether Freeling starts as a rookie remains to be seen. But if Walker was signed as a stopgap at left tackle following Ekwonu’s patellar tendon surgery, Freeling was drafted as a long-term answer at tackle. Freeling began his Georgia career as a swing tackle, so he has experience at both right and left tackle. That gives the Panthers flexibility as they evaluate Ekwonu, both in terms of his return from a significant injury and his place in the organization’s plans as he enters a contract year. There are also questions surrounding Moton’s future at right tackle as the veteran enters his age-32 season. Moton for years had been the team’s Ironman, with his streak of 120 consecutive games (and 104 starts) finally ending in 2024. Moton, who has dealt with chronic knee issues, signed a two-year extension that will take him through the 2027 season. “Retirement’s not on my mind right now,” Moton said this week. “I feel great running around with all the young guys. I’m feeling young. I feel like I’m moving well and I’m feeling like, shoot, I’m still in my prime, right? I don’t feel like I’m slowing down.”
With the arrival of Brazzell, Legette lands in the “losers” category for the second year in a row. It was easy to see the Panthers’ selection of Tetairoa McMillan with the eighth pick last year as an indictment of Legette, who has struggled with drops, field awareness and general inconsistency. While McMillan was on his way to Offensive Rookie of the Year honors, Jalen Coker was supplanting Legette as WR2. Legette’s status hasn’t changed that much with the addition of Brazzell. If he can clean up some of the things that have slowed his development, he’ll be in the WR rotation. If not, he won’t — and becomes a potential trade candidate. The difference now is there’s another intriguing option at receiver, although Brazzell is not without his warts. He ran a limited route tree at Tennessee, where nearly 50 percent of his routes last season were either a hitch or a go. But Brazzell’s big-play ability — he came down with 13 of his 23 targets of 20-plus yards in 2025 — should light a fire under Legette. Or not.

Veteran wide receiver Chase Claypool is attending the Green Bay Packers rookie minicamp on a tryout basis. Claypool, 27, was present at the Packers’ practice Friday in Green Bay alongside their six draft picks, 10 undrafted rookie signings, 13 current young players and eight other tryout players.
Claypool, a 2020 second-round pick of the Pittsburgh Steelers out of Notre Dame, was a PFWA all-rookie team selection in 2020, when he had 873 receiving yards and 11 total touchdowns. He was traded to the Chicago Bears at the 2022 trade deadline, then dealt to the Miami Dolphins less than a year later. He hasn’t appeared in an NFL game since 2023. Claypool suffered a toe injury during training camp in August 2024 with the Buffalo Bills and was subsequently released.
Claypool has 175 catches for 2,261 yards, 13 receiving touchdowns and two rushing touchdowns in 58 career games with the Steelers, Bears and Dolphins.

full_text:
Deshaun Watson (right) was usually first in line as the Browns' quarterbacks rotated through drills during their first minicamp practice. Nick Cammett / Getty Images
Cleveland Browns coach Todd Monken said Friday that while he’d like to name a starting quarterback before the team opens training camp in late July, it’s still too early for any decisions.
Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders are the primary competitors for the job. Watson missed all of last season while recovering from a twice-torn right Achilles tendon, and Sanders started the final seven games of his rookie season under former coach Kevin Stefanski.
With the offense new in structure and in personnel at almost every position, Monken said he’s hoping a clear winner emerges. But, despite one report indicating Watson is the favorite, Monken reiterated in an interview on WKRK-FM in Cleveland that he’s not ready to make a call on the starter just yet.
“It’s my job to let it play out,” Monken said.
The Browns held a three-day voluntary minicamp ahead of last week’s draft. In the one practice open to reporters, Watson was usually first in line as the quarterbacks rotated through drills, but Monken said the practice script called for Sanders to take more total reps.
After that first practice last week, Monken said the order of quarterback reps will continue to change as the Browns go forward.
“I’m not there yet, so I can’t say (there’s a leader),” Monken said during an in-studio appearance on “The Ken Carman Show.” “We’ve been on the field three days.”
The Browns’ first organized team activity practice is scheduled for May 19. The team can have up to 10 OTA practices ahead of a mid-June mandatory minicamp that wraps up the offseason program.
Cleveland added sixth-round rookie Taylen Green to the quarterback room during last week’s draft. For now, Watson, Sanders and 2025 third-round pick Dillon Gabriel are participating in the second phase of the team’s offseason program, which includes offensive installation meetings and on-the-field drill work, but not in competitive situations. When OTAs begin, one practice per week will be open to reporters.
The Browns didn’t add a veteran to the group in March. In February, Monken said he believed there would be an “open competition” throughout the spring and possibly the summer, but he wouldn’t set a firm deadline for a decision.
Monken’s comments Friday matched his previous stance of letting the players decide who plays and giving all involved opportunities, but not equal reps, as the competition progresses.

full_text:
The Broncos selected Justin Joly in the fifth round of this year's NFL Draft. Jim Dedmon / Imagn Images
Jim Mora could sense the excitement in Justin Joly’s voice, as if the lanky teenager was ready to hurdle himself through the phone.
Mora had developed a relationship with Joly while recruiting him to play football at UConn and was preparing one day to visit the young athlete at Iona Prep, the Catholic high school located just outside New York City. Joly had something he had to show the veteran coach.
“He was so excited that he could finally dunk,” Mora said with a laugh during a recent phone conversation. “He couldn’t wait to show me that he could dunk. When I got there, it wasn’t the dunk that was impressive to me. The impressive part was that I’m watching him hold a basketball and it looks like a tennis ball in his hand.”
Broncos general manager George Paton issued a warning last week after the Broncos selected Joly, a 6-foot-4, 241-pound tight end, in the fifth round of the NFL Draft.
“Don’t shake his hand,” Paton said. “He’ll try to break it every time.”
It was advice Gavin Locklear, the tight ends coach at North Carolina State, could have used in late 2023 as he hosted Joly on an official visit, the player having entered the transfer portal in search of a step up in competition.
“I shake his hand, and he’s got these ginormous hands,” Locklear said. “He’s got 10-½-inch hands and the strongest grip in the world. … He just engulfs the football.”
The Broncos are counting on Joly to do just that. In search of a target who can help lift the pass-catching profile of the tight end room, Denver last week made the biggest draft investment in the position since Sean Payton became head coach in 2023. The Broncos also used one of their seventh-round picks on Utah tight end Dallen Bentley, who had a breakout senior season in 2025 with 620 receiving yards and six touchdowns.
Payton, after the draft, labeled Joly as an ‘F’ move tight end, a receiving target who could be deployed across the formation in an effort to exploit mismatches in opposing defenses.
“He’s smart, so he can handle a lot of volume in terms of packages for him,” said Mora, the current coach at Colorado State, whose career includes more than two decades in the NFL. “He can play a lot of spots. I know Sean will create matchup issues because Sean is great at it.”
Payton has helped pull highly productive seasons out of tight ends throughout his coaching career, from Jeremy Shockey and Jimmy Graham to Ben Watson and Jared Cook. That statistical profile hasn’t existed to this point in Payton’s Broncos tenure, though. Denver ranks last since 2023 in tight end receiving yards (1,564), last in receptions (168), last in targets (248) and 30th in air yards per target (5.07), according to TruMedia.
In Joly, the Broncos have added a player who caught at least 43 passes in each of his last three college seasons. His seven touchdown receptions last season were second among all FBS tight ends behind New York Jets first-round pick Kenyon Sadiq. He dropped only one pass while being North Carolina State’s most-targeted receiver in 2025. He did it while showcasing a trait that could be exactly what Denver has been missing.
“He’s as good at catching in traffic as any receiver I’ve seen in my 25 years of coaching,” said Joe Spagnolo, Joly’s coach at Iona Prep. “He does not need a lot of room.”
The perfect illustration came last season, in a November matchup with Florida State. The Wolfpack held a 14-11 lead with less than two minutes remaining in the game. They faced a fourth-and-6 at the FSU 12-yard line. Pick up a first down, and NC State could melt the clock away. Fail, and the Seminoles would have ample time to drive for a tying or winning score.
“Justin came over to me and was like, ‘Throw me the ball,'” Locklear said. “It just so happened to where our offensive coordinator had a play he really liked that had Justin singled up on the backside. The rest was history after that.”
The play called for Joly to be split out wide to the left, matching him up with FSU cornerback Shamar Arnoux. The defensive back backpedaled quickly and anticipated Joly’s cut toward the pylon in the front of the end zone. Joly, though, adjusted his route to keep Arnoux behind them as he jumped for the ball. Joly, with the corner draped all over him, gripped the ball as he tumbled to the ground, securing his second touchdown of the game and the victory for the Wolfpack.
Who else 🤷‍♂️ #1Pack1Goal pic.twitter.com/XZ9XKoFN21
— NC State Football (@PackFootball) November 22, 2025
Mora, who has stayed in close contact with Joly since the tight end transferred, caught a replay of the score later and was quickly transported back to the times when UConn would “put him over at the X and watch him snatch the ball off a corner’s head.”
The vision of a player who looks to be cut straight from tight end central casting, though, wasn’t always to see with Joly. Basketball was his first love, but he tended to burn too hot on the court, at times.
“You know those basketball kids who are too aggressive to where they can’t really play basketball anymore? He’s the perfect example of that,” said Jamel Wright Jr., a friend of the Joly family who helped coach Justin as a youth football player. “He’s going too hard on the court and he’s beating up on some of his teammates during practice and stuff. That just naturally gravitated him toward the football field.”
Joly’s football path took shape while playing for the Harlem Jets, a youth program that practices on weeknights at Wagner Playground, a patch of grass located just a stone’s throw away from the Harlem River. It’s become something of a Field of Dreams, only set within a concrete jungle instead of an Iowa cornfield.
“It’s really a soccer field that they line up for us to play football in the fall,” said Jamel Wright Sr., better known as Coach Mel to the players and families he’s worked with since founding the program back in 2005. “The older kids would have the larger portion on the end because they’d need a little more space. Then, a few steps in, you’d have 10U, 9U, 7U. It’s like a magic trick, man. You’ve got some guys going upfield, some guys going downfield, other guys practicing going across the field.”
Joly came to embrace the contact and the camaraderie. He played primarily running back and linebacker on the Jets’ 14U team that would travel across the Tri-State area — and sometimes beyond — to face the best competition possible. Ultimately, though, he became the solution to whatever roster problem the Jets had that needed solving during a given practice or game.
“Justin was always one of those versatile guys who could play just about anywhere for you,” Wright Sr. said.
That rang true as Joly’s football path took shape at Iona Prep, where he began playing on the varsity team as a wide receiver during his sophomore season. By the time he was a senior, Joly had given up basketball completely so that his offseasons could be spent in the weight room, Spagnolo said. He was now 6-foot-3 and almost 200 pounds and was becoming a nightmare for defenses to cover.
Some teams resorted to extreme measures. They would bracket their coverages Joly’s way, double-teaming him constantly, trying to force quarterbacks to look anywhere else.
“It got to the point where we’d put him in the backfield and just give him the ball,” Spagnolo said. “At 6-3, 6-4, 200-some-odd pounds, he wasn’t your typical, running-back-looking guy, but his skill set is so unique where he had this huge growth spurt and has this tall, long body, but he still had the agility of a running back. We’d get through the first quarter and, if we weren’t getting him touches through the air, it was, ‘Alright, let’s get him in the backfield. Let’s get him touches. Let’s figure out a creative way to get him the ball.'”
Built in the mold of Jonnu Smith, but needs to refine his route running.

Claypool, a 2020 second-round pick of the Pittsburgh Steelers out of Notre Dame, was a PFWA all-rookie team selection in 2020, when he had 873 receiving yards and 11 total touchdowns. Claypool has 175 catches for 2,261 yards, 13 receiving touchdowns and two rushing touchdowns in 58 career games with the Steelers, Bears and Dolphins.

full_text:
Quarterback Kyron Drones is among the undrafted rookies the Packers will evaluate. Butch Dill / Getty Images
GREEN BAY, Wis. — Undrafted players don’t get much shine this time of year, but you never know when they’ll be called into action once games start counting.
The Green Bay Packers had several undrafted guys play key roles last season, including cornerback Keisean Nixon, former backup running back Emanuel Wilson and former special teams ace and reserve safety Zayne Anderson. This coming season, players like defensive tackle Nazir Stackhouse, edge rusher Brenton Cox Jr. and running back Chris Brooks, none of whom heard their names called in their respective drafts, could play vital roles for the Packers.
The Packers signed 11 undrafted free agents to fill out their 90-man roster after this year’s draft. A rookie undrafted free agent has made Green Bay’s Week 1 53-man roster in 21 straight seasons. Who might that player (or players) be this time around? Let’s break down the class, with rookie minicamp kicking off on Friday morning.
Kyron Drones, QB, Virginia Tech (22.8 years old, 6-foot-1 ⅝, 226 pounds)
Drones enters a potentially advantageous situation, with no draft picks or recent free-agent signings at quarterback to compete against. Veteran Desmond Ridder and reserve/future signing Kyle McCord are ahead of him on the depth chart and the Packers are likely to take only two quarterbacks on the 53-man roster, but a practice squad spot could be up for grabs. Drones completed 178 of 315 passes for 1,919 yards and 17 touchdowns while starting all 12 games for the Hokies last season. He also ran 170 times for 644 yards and nine scores. He adds the running element now absent from Green Bay’s quarterback room after Malik Willis left in free agency.
Jaden Nixon, RB, UCF (age not listed, 5-9 ⅛, 199)
The Packers will also have a competition for the backup running back spot this offseason. If Brooks wins that battle and MarShawn Lloyd again struggles to stay healthy, there could be a vacancy at Brooks’ former spot at third on the depth chart. Nixon ran 143 times for 919 yards and 12 touchdowns at Western Michigan in 2024, before transferring to UCF and running only 71 times for 554 yards and seven touchdowns in 12 games. He was, however, an All-Big 12 honorable mention as a kick returner after averaging 23.1 yards on 19 returns with one touchdown. He is also the second cousin of former NFL great Adrian Peterson.
J. Michael Sturdivant, WR, Florida (23.6, 6-2 ½, 210)
The Athletic’s Dane Brugler had a sixth-round grade on Sturdivant, so he could be one to watch come training camp. Sturdivant, who ran a 4.4 40 at the combine, joins the crowded back end of a receiver room headlined by Christian Watson, Jayden Reed and Matthew Golden. Sturdivant caught 65 passes for 755 yards and seven touchdowns at Cal in 2022, but never replicated that production in two seasons at UCLA and one at Florida. His signing was first reported by CBS Sports (all of the others have been announced by respective college programs).
Here’s Brugler’s scouting report: “Sturdivant accelerates well for his size to stack vertically and gain a step on top of coverage. He is more smooth than sudden in his route running, and his momentum can get away from him at times, which is why he is at his best on runway routes. His drop rate improved each season (8.3 percent in 2024 to just 3.6 percent in ‘25), and he gives his quarterback some wiggle room with ball placement.”
RJ Maryland, TE, SMU (21.8, 6-3 ½, 238)
Brugler had a “seventh round/free agent” grade on Maryland, so he’ll be another to watch in a tight end room that lost John FitzPatrick to a torn Achilles tendon late last season (he remains an unrestricted free agent) and didn’t add anyone from outside the building in free agency or the draft. Maryland is the son of Russell Maryland, the No. 1 pick in the 1991 NFL Draft, who won two national titles as a defensive tackle at Miami and three Super Bowls with the Dallas Cowboys.
Brugler’s scouting report (on the younger Maryland): “Though he inherited his size from his father, an NFL defensive tackle, his speed came from somewhere else — he can threaten the seams and find open pockets. His top speed of 22.70 mph at the combine was faster than several receivers, including Carnell Tate (22.68) and Chris Brazzell II (22.59). His tracking and body adjustments are strengths, although crowded catch points will give him trouble.”
Eni Falayi, TE, Wake Forest (age not listed, 6-4 ⅞, 249)
Falayi played for UMass and Utah Tech before transferring to Wake Forest, where he caught 21 passes for 228 yards and two touchdowns last season. General manager Brian Gutekunst said after the draft that the one thing he wanted to add was a blocking tight end. Falayi fills that need with his build.
Dillon Wade, OL, Auburn (23.9, 6-3, 316)
Wade also had a “seventh round/free agent” grade from Brugler, whose scouting report of the former Tigers offensive lineman is as follows:
“With his initial quickness and movement ability, Wade can quickly gain the upper hand in pass pro or be an asset on pulls/climbs in the run game. He fits with adequate technique, but spotty power allows his balance to be disrupted by defenders who know what they are doing. In the run game, he gets where he is going in a hurry but doesn’t consistently uproot his targets.”
Wade started at every offensive line spot except center over the last two years at Auburn and started 37 games in the last three seasons there.
Josh Gesky, OL, Illinois (23.3, 6-5 ⅛, 308)
Brugler ranked Gesky two spots higher than Wade on his list of top offensive guards in the draft. He started 26 games at left guard over the last two seasons at Illinois. The Packers only drafted one offensive lineman, Kentucky interior offensive lineman Jager Burton, so Wade and Gesky could push for roster spots on a team whose offensive line depth doesn’t appear to be a strong suit despite Gutekunst’s recent vote of confidence.
Brugler: “He was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes at age 6, but scouts say he manages it well with the staff (always has a water or Gatorade on him). Though his redirect skills are marginal, he has adequate feet and eager hands to set up shop and get into a punch-ready position. He is a coach-pleaser, with a blue-collar mindset as a worker … Gesky can do a better job with his flexibility to create leverage, but his natural strength and torque allow him to cover up in the run game or anchor in pass pro. His pro-day workout created a buzz among scouts.”
Dylan Barrett, OL, Iowa State (age not listed, 6-4 ⅜, 326)
Barrett spent four seasons at Wisconsin before starting at left guard the last two seasons for Iowa State.
Nyjalik Kelly, Edge, UCF (21.5, 6-5 ¼, 263)
Kelly, who received a “seventh round/free agent” grade from Brugler, had 17 tackles for loss, 8.5 sacks, five forced fumbles, five passes defensed and one interception over the last two seasons at UCF. A roster spot at edge rusher will be hard to come by, even with Micah Parsons expected to be sidelined for the first chunk of the season, but Kelly possesses the physical traits and college production to push the likes of Collin Oliver, Barryn Sorrell, Arron Mosby, Cox and fourth-round rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton in camp.
Brugler: “Kelly has a super-long frame, and his arms measured the longest among the 35 edge rushers invited to the NFL combine. He uses his extension to stack blocks and battle through traffic versus the run, although wild tackling attempts lead to misses. He also uses his length to long-arm blockers and set up bull-rush attempts. However, he doesn’t show much of a rush plan and relies more on hustle than skill, which leaves him out of position.”
TJ Quinn, LB, Louisville (age not listed, 6-0 ¼, 225)
Quinn earned third-team All-ACC honors after posting 95 tackles, eight tackles for loss, three sacks, four passes defensed and two picks last season. He was also durable, playing in 53 games over the last four…

title: Execs unfiltered on every AFC team's draft: Are things finally looking up for Jets, Raiders? Is it really OK to feel good about the Jets? Meanwhile, reviews were mixed on the Bills', Jaguars' and Texans' draft classes. Mike Sando 35
summary:
Fernando Mendoza (right) is officially a Raider. Meanwhile David Bailey (center) and Kadyn Proctor headed draft classes praised by many around the league. Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; Photos: Ethan Miller / Getty Images, Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
After dissecting NFC teams’ drafts Thursday , we’re back with NFL executives’ insights into how all 16 AFC teams handled the annual player selection process.
Did the Buffalo Bills make wise use of all those picks (10) after trading
full_text:
Fernando Mendoza (right) is officially a Raider. Meanwhile David Bailey (center) and Kadyn Proctor headed draft classes praised by many around the league. Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; Photos: Ethan Miller / Getty Images, Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
After dissecting NFC teams’ drafts Thursday , we’re back with NFL executives’ insights into how all 16 AFC teams handled the annual player selection process.
Did the Buffalo Bills make wise use of all those picks (10) after trading down? Was the Cleveland Browns’ draft as good as the analysts suggested? Do the Houston Texans care what anyone thinks? Should the Indianapolis Colts regret the Sauce Gardner trade? Does anyone have anything good to say about Jaguars general manager James Gladstone? Is it really OK to feel good about the New York Jets?
Execs answer these and many more questions during my annual draft review.
For each team, we’ve included where it ranked in draft capital used (calculated using an NFL analytical model) and in Dane Brugler’s favorite classes , along with how many times it traded up or down during the draft (excluding deals that involved veteran players).
Draft capital rank: 11th | Brugler’s rank: 11th | Trades up/down: 1/0
The Ravens continued their recent trend of targeting less-premium positions in the first round, inviting an interesting philosophical discussion.
Guard Olaivavega Ioane (No. 14 this year) joins safety Malaki Starks (No. 27 in 2025), safety Kyle Hamilton (No. 14 in 2022) and center Tyler Linderbaum (No. 25 in 2022) among the recent Baltimore first-rounders fitting that mold.
All qualify as solid or even spectacular players.
Execs see Ioane as a high-odds prospect as well.
“Really good, good player — probably the best guard in the draft,” one said.
A thick, nasty mauler on track to be a long-term NFL starter.
The problem, if there is one, is that teams are generally less likely to re-sign players at these positions once their rookie contracts expire (Hamilton, the lone superstar among the group, did sign a four-year, $100.4 million deal before last season).
“The positional-value talk before the draft was interesting — teams said you can throw that out this year with the premium players playing non-premium positions,” another exec said. “(Sonny) Styles, (Caleb) Downs, (Jeremiyah) Love all fit that. Guards are expensive now, so it’s not as bad to pick up their options.
“Indy made it work with Quenton Nelson, and he was picked a lot higher (No. 6) than Ioane.”
Linderbaum’s case is instructive. He was everything the Ravens could have hoped, starting 66 of a possible 68 career games, earning three consecutive Pro Bowl honors and ranking fourth in Pro Football Focus’ grading for centers last season. But Baltimore declined his fifth-year option last spring because the value ($23.4 million) is tied to all offensive linemen (not centers, specifically). When his deal expired after four years, the Raiders signed him to a three-year, $81 million deal, resetting the market at the position by roughly 50 percent.
No one faults Baltimore for failing to meet that steep price, but if Ioane leaves in four years, no one should be shocked, either.
The void at center endures for Baltimore.
After using the first-round pick on Ioane and a second-rounder on an edge rusher (Zion Young), the Ravens watched two centers come off the board — Logan Jones to Chicago at No. 57, Jake Slaughter to the Chargers at No. 63 — before they were back on the clock at No. 80 and took receiver Ja’Kobi Lane.
Garrett Bradbury, acquired by Chicago from New England this offseason, would be a logical trade target if the Bears like what they see from Jones, the center they drafted in the second round. Bradbury played at NC State when current Ravens offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford coached the position for the Wolfpack.
“Baltimore is going to let everybody who can snap the ball try,” an exec said. “That would not be a bad trade. If I’m Chicago, I would not trade him until I know what I have with Logan Jones and know he is the guy.”
The Ravens doubled up on receiver and tight end in the third through fifth rounds.
“Ja’Kobi Lane is really talented — he has ability, but he’s really inconsistent,” an exec said of the Ravens’ third-round receiver. “(Matthew) Hibner is a good route-running tight end, has a little speed, catches it well, is perfect for them to develop. But he doesn’t have the body control that (Isaiah) Likely had.”
Draft capital rank: 25th | Brugler’s rank: 22nd | Trades up/down: 1/6
Execs admired the Bills’ ability to maneuver around the board while making a league-high seven in-draft trades, but reviews were mixed regarding the players Buffalo wound up selecting.
“Those picks you gain, whether it’s a third or fourth or something later, they were not going to net you any (good) players in this draft,” one exec said.
Time will tell on that front. The team drafted 10 players, tied for third-most in the league, and used its second-rounder to acquire receiver DJ Moore from Chicago.
“I do think there’s some element of regime change with (coach) Joe Brady and (GM) Brandon (Beane) wanting to make this his team and put in his stamp on it,” another exec said. “(Having) more picks probably helps do that. But again, this was a weird draft, in that it was terrible at the top and terrible at the bottom.”
“There was no sweet spot to accumulate picks,” this exec added. “I do not really begrudge anybody’s strategy in this draft, because I don’t know what you were supposed to do to be effective.”
The Bills traded down from 26 to 28, then to 31, then to 35, where they selected Clemson edge rusher T.J. Parker.
“The issue I have is, they took guys who have questionable play style,” a third exec said. “If you asked them what their identity is, they might say tough, physical, all these things. But you look at the guys they drafted, and it’s not that.”
“I was a big fan of Parker,” a different exec said. “Real young kid. Huge upside. The problem is, those Clemson defensive linemen, they just haven’t really developed, so there’s a little bit of a concern there.”
Still learning some moves, but offers playmaking potential against both run and pass.
Draft capital rank: 28th | Brugler’s rank: 24th | Trades up/down: 0/1
Execs applauded the Bengals’ decision to trade the 10th pick to the Giants for nose tackle Dexter Lawrence. They saw it as the surest way available for the Bengals to upgrade their defense and demonstrate to quarterback Joe Burrow that the team was serious, two huge priorities this offseason.
“This is like the NBA when you are trying to acquire guys to keep your star who is going to leave happy,” one exec said. “Is it expensive? Sure, but there is no price on keeping Burrow happy. Drafting Rueben Bain does not make Burrow happy.”
The Bengals also traded down with the Jets, who selected quarterback Cade Klubnik with Cincinnati’s pick in the fourth round. That deal helped the Bengals land receiver Colbie Young along with center Connor Lew.
“Young is legit — he’s big, and he’s got good hips and really good instincts for route running,” another exec said. “He is an outside receiver, though, so there is no one who can play the slot for them unless they put Ja’Marr Chase in there. It’s a helluva value pick. I just don’t know how you play all three at once.”
After effectively landing Lawrence with the 10th pick, the Bengals addressed defense with their own second- and third-round picks. They already added Boye Mafe, Bryan Cook and Jonathan Allen to deals totaling $45.9 million in average salary after letting edge rushers Trey Hendrickson and Joseph Ossai leave in free agency.
“Dexter Lawrence would be a top-five pick in this draft even at his age,” a third exec said. “There is no one like him in this draft. He can change their defense, coupled with what they did in free agency.”
How could the Bengals have handled the Lawrence trade better? A fourth exec suggested they could have tried to involve a…

summary:

Kansas City Chiefs vice president of player personnel Ryne Nutt said Monday that the team was “very excited” about the group of undrafted free agents coming in for this weekend’s rookie minicamp.
“We think this is going to be one of the better (undrafted) free-agent classes we’ve had,” Nutt said.
It’s worth remembering this to start: UDFAs
full_text:
Cincinnati wide receiver Jeff Caldwell was given a fifth- to sixth-round grade by Dane Brugler, The Athletic's lead draft analyst. Ron Jenkins / Getty Images
Kansas City Chiefs vice president of player personnel Ryne Nutt said Monday that the team was “very excited” about the group of undrafted free agents coming in for this weekend’s rookie minicamp.
“We think this is going to be one of the better (undrafted) free-agent classes we’ve had,” Nutt said.
It’s worth remembering this to start: UDFAs face long odds of making it. There are still exceptions each year, including players like linebacker Cooper McDonald, who made the Chiefs’ initial 53-man roster last season after coming in as an UDFA from TCU.
So, who might have a chance to play his way onto K.C.’s roster this year?
From looking at the Chiefs’ reported and expected UDFA signings, here’s a list of eight players who could have the best shot.
The Athletic ’s Dane Brugler ranked Anthony as this class’ 36th-best edge rusher, saying he has a “best-case outcome of an Arden Key-type career.” Anthony had 15 career sacks for the Blue Devils and has good size (6-foot-5, 258 pounds), though Brugler notes he’s only an average-twitch athlete who had some struggles going against stronger blockers. The Chiefs’ depth chart seems like it still could be one pass rusher short, so Anthony has that going for him as he looks to impress the coaches.
Brugler says Bissainthe (pronounced bih-SAINT) is an aggressive tackler and someone whose energy could help him stand out on special teams. The 6-1, 225-pound Bissainthe can struggle to get off blocks, but he still has enough size/speed combo to be worth a look — especially for a Chiefs team that could be seeking competition for a back-of-the-roster linebacker spot.
The Leawood, Kan., native and Rockhurst High graduate will be showcasing for his hometown team. Gyllenborg is an athletic specimen — he actually made The Athletic writer Bruce Feldman’s “Freaks List” in August — while boasting 21.6 mph speed and a 37-inch vertical jump. He needs to work on his blocking, and drops have been an issue, but the 6-5, 249-pounder has enough physical tools to earn a long look as the Chiefs sort through options behind mainstays Travis Kelce and Noah Gray.
Nwankpa (pronounced WAUM-puh), who is Brugler’s 23rd-ranked safety, was a three-year starter for Iowa and has good size and speed at 6-2, 208 pounds. He didn’t always show the best instincts, however, and showing off as a special teams standout could be his best path toward a potential roster spot. The Chiefs, as mentioned in our latest depth-chart piece, suddenly have a roster glut in the secondary, meaning Nwankpa potentially faces a tougher path than others on this list.
The 5-11, 198-pound Ott finds a familiar home with the Chiefs, as he’ll link back up with Chiefs running backs coach DeMarco Murray, who was his position coach at Oklahoma. Ott is a bit of an enigma; he had a strong first two seasons at Cal (and also made Feldman’s “Freaks List” ) before struggling in his final two campaigns with injuries. Brugler had him as the 21st-ranked running back in this class, describing him as a “bursty, one-cut runner” who could potentially thrive on third downs and on special teams as a kick returner. Questions about injuries and his toughness will be obstacles for Ott to overcome as he looks to get into the team’s running back competition behind Kenneth Walker III and rookie Emmett Johnson.
General manager Brett Veach said before the draft he hoped to come away with two defensive tackles; he ended up getting only one, while using a first-round pick on Peter Woods . That’s good news for Brevard, who joins a team that looks like it could use one more rotational player on its defensive interior. Brevard, at 6-2 and 343 pounds, is Brugler’s 50th-ranked defensive tackle and often flashed in college as a powerful run-stopper.
NT Cole Brevard taking on four blockers at POA on third-and-1 pic.twitter.com/UyHFGAznn5
— Ted Nguyen (@FB_FilmAnalysis) August 30, 2025
Brugler was high on Singleton, giving him a fifth- to sixth-round draft grade while ranking him as the 15th-best safety in this class. Singleton looks the part at 6-3, 205 pounds, and he led Nebraska last season in passes defended and interceptions. He’s not always fluid with his movements, though, and like Nwankpa, could see special teams as his best opportunity to make an early impression.
Caldwell will arrive in K.C. as the freakiest of the “Freaks List” alums. His relative athletic score — a metric used to evaluate prospects’ measurements — ranked a perfect 10.0; it’s the second-best mark of any receiver since 1987, with only Calvin Johnson ahead of him.

Behind Calvin Johnson, pending pro day. https://t.co/ouxCKYCrgp pic.twitter.com/GK7dXNMK8s

Brugler ranked Caldwell as his 26th-best receiver and gave him a fifth- to sixth-round grade. The 6-5, 216-pound Caldwell ran a 4.31-second 40-yard dash at the NFL combine with a 42-inch vertical jump, but he remains raw at the position and also needs to show he can play with better strength. He might be a project, but Caldwell could also pay off huge with the right development system and coaching staff. The Chiefs appear to have a few openings at wideout on the end of their roster, so Caldwell appears to be in an ideal situation if he proves to be a quick learner.

title: Rams post-draft roster analysis: How the rookies fill out the depth chart The Rams come out of the draft with just a five-man rookie class, all of whom add depth but are unlikely to begin the season as starters. Nate Atkins 2
summary:
Max Klare joins a crowded Rams tight end room but could add real value going into his second season. Steph Chambers / Getty Images
The Los Angeles Rams didn’t take the approach to this year’s NFL Draft that many were expecting. After a narrow loss in the NFC Championship Game, a joyous return for an 18th NFL season for Matthew Stafford and an all-in push in free agency, they went to the draft to fill out their depth and plan for the future.
That started with the selection of Alabama quarterback
full_text:
Max Klare joins a crowded Rams tight end room but could add real value going into his second season. Steph Chambers / Getty Images
The Los Angeles Rams didn’t take the approach to this year’s NFL Draft that many were expecting. After a narrow loss in the NFC Championship Game, a joyous return for an 18th NFL season for Matthew Stafford and an all-in push in free agency, they went to the draft to fill out their depth and plan for the future.
That started with the selection of Alabama quarterback Ty Simpson at No. 13 and continued with a class of just five players, the smallest general manager Les Snead has ever had. But that doesn’t mean they didn’t fill some important spots, as the Rams needed to add depth and lock in some cost-controlled deals while balancing re-signing a handful of key players entering contract years.
With offseason practices starting soon, this is a good time to take an updated look at the depth chart.
Starter: Matthew Stafford Top backup: Ty Simpson Depth: Stetson Bennett
Simpson was the Rams’ big splash in this draft, but he will arrive to a competition with Bennett to replace Jimmy Garoppolo as Stafford’s backup. The Rams were prepared to take Simpson even if Garoppolo returned, a team source told The Athletic , so this will be an opportunity to let him compete and earn something early; the starting role is blocked until Stafford retires. It doesn’t completely shut the door on a Garoppolo return, but that’s considered unlikely at this point.
The time on the bench could be beneficial to Simpson, who started just 15 games at Alabama. He stood out to the Rams, particularly in their secret pre-draft meetings, as someone as excited to learn as he is to play after becoming the rare college quarterback to sit before his chance to start one season at Alabama.
He’ll enter a lab of learning behind Stafford and from coach Sean McVay, offensive coordinator Nathan Scheelhaase, quarterbacks coach Dave Ragone and assistant head coach Kliff Kingsbury, a former NFL quarterback who helped develop Kyler Murray and Jayden Daniels as rookies. The giant question of when Simpson will see the field remains a mystery, but the Rams are confident that the longer he sits, the better he will be when that chance arrives.
Starter: Kyren Williams Top backup: Blake Corum Depth: Ronnie Rivers, Jarquez Hunter
The Rams left their running back room untouched this offseason, and for good reason. Williams had 1,252 yards and 10 rushing touchdowns last season for his third straight 1,100-yard campaign. Corum added 746 yards and six scores in a breakout Year 2.
Expect this to be more of a 50-50 split this season, with Williams as a primary third-down back and between-the-tackles runner and Corum more of a change-of-pace option with explosive capabilities. Hunter will have to wait his turn again, but last year’s fourth-round pick could be valuable if either Williams or Corum has to miss time, which neither did last season.
Starters: Puka Nacua, Davante Adams Top backup: CJ Daniels Depth: Konata Mumpfield, Jordan Whittington, Xavier Smith
Many expected the Rams to prioritize wide receiver in the draft as they were lacking depth behind Nacua and Adams, each of whom missed three games last season. Instead, they waited until the sixth round to take Daniels out of Miami.
Daniels is a strong fit for a third receiver role after blocking in one of college football’s most physical offenses. Time will tell if he can be that injury replacement for a top option, as he caught just 50 passes for 557 yards and seven touchdowns in 13 games last season, though he did play six college seasons.
Mumpfield, Whittington and Smith will all compete with Daniels for the third spot and should have their moments to showcase different skill sets. If a reliable third option doesn’t emerge early in the season, this could be a spot the Rams trade for in October now that their 2027 draft picks are back open for business with Simpson filling the need for a future quarterback.
Starter: Terrance Ferguson Top backup: Colby Parkinson Depth: Tyler Higbee, Davis Allen, Max Klare
The 13-personnel revolution is here to stay. Los Angeles rolled back a four-man tight end room that had every member score at least three times last season, and yet it still added another option in Klare in the second round out of Ohio State. That’s what happens when a team leads the league in two- and three-tight end sets and finishes No. 1 in scoring offense.
Klare has run-after-the-catch ability and could see some designs, but the hope is that this is a room Ferguson takes the lead in after redshirting much of last season. Klare is more of a future piece at a developmental position and could prove valuable in a year when Parkinson and Allen hit free agency and Higbee turns 34.
Starters: Alaric Jackson, Warren McClendon Jr. Top backup: Keagan Trost Depth: David Quessenberry
Even with the retirement of Rob Havenstein, the Rams were able to return five starters on their offensive line. Trost arrives in the third round out of Missouri as a strong run blocker in wide-zone concepts who can bump out to either tackle spot if needed. The Rams also like Quessenberry’s experience at both tackle spots. This will be a big season for McClendon, who could build off last year’s breakout to earn a hefty payday in free agency.
Starters: Steve Avila, Kevin Dotson Top backup: Justin Dedich Depth: Keagan Trost, Beaux Limmer
Los Angeles had a solid depth piece on the interior in Dedich, and will now add Trost to the mix. If Trost gets an opportunity to play, he could earn a chance to replace either Avila or Dotson if one leaves in free agency next year. The guards are the engines for this team in the run game, and they’re also critical to keeping the pocket secure for a 38-year-old quarterback in Stafford.
Starter: Coleman Shelton Top backup: Steve Avila Depth: Dylan McMahon
The Rams liked their setup for center entering the draft, with Shelton running the show and Avila having the ability to bump inside if needed. The arrival of Trost makes that more of a possibility now, as he can fill in at left guard when necessary.
Starters: Poona Ford, Kobie Turner Top backup: Braden Fiske Depth: Tim Keenan III, Tyler Davis, Ty Hamilton
The Rams like the mix they have here of a run stopper in Ford and pass rushers in Turner and Fiske, who can also bump outside. Their run defense fell off too much last season when Ford had to leave the field, so now Keenan arrives at 6-foot-1, 327 pounds to help out. That depth could be important as Ford turns 31 in November and needs a reasonable snap count to remain fresh and handle all the double-teams that come his way.
Starters: Jared Verse, Byron Young Top backup: Josaiah Stewart Depth: Keir Thomas II
The Rams chose not to take an edge rusher this year despite Turner, who plays some on the edge, and Young both entering contract years. That is, in part, due to the impressive play in a small sample last season by Stewart, a 2025 third-rounder. With Turner and Fiske able to play outside, the rotation should remain steady around Verse, who the Rams hope can take a surge from Pro Bowler to more of a closer for the defense in his third season.
Starters: Nate Landman, Omar Speights Top backup: Grant Stuard Depth: Shaun Dolac
The Rams found a diamond in the rough last year in Landman, which worked out quickly enough to ink him to a three-year extension. That let them continue a trend of not valuing this spot in the draft. They did sign Stuard to round out the depth, though his biggest contributions should come on special teams. The same is true for Dolac, who is recovering from a PCL injury. Speights will start at the other linebacker spot in a more limited role with the high rate of dime personnel the Rams use, which should only increase with Trent McDuffie’s arrival in the secondary.

full_text:
Could Kansei Matsuzawa be the Raiders' kicker in 2026? Marco Garcia / Imagn Images
The Las Vegas Raiders left the NFL Draft with several spots still to fill on their roster. They addressed many of those in the past few days with a large group of undrafted free agents, adding 17 more players since the draft’s conclusion on Saturday.
The first look at the group, along with No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza and the Raiders’ nine other draftees, will come this weekend when the team hosts its rookie minicamp.
No undrafted rookies made Las Vegas’ initial 53-man roster last season, but both tight end Carter Runyon and defensive back Greedy Vance earned playing time later in the year. With depth needed on a rebuilt roster, this crop could see similar opportunities — some could even make the team out of camp.
Here’s a ranking of the UDFAs with the best chance to stick around with the Raiders in 2026, from least likely to most. (Positional rankings are according to “The Beast”):
Lauter had a productive college career for Boise State, where he was teammates with Ashton Jeanty for three seasons. He earned All-Mountain West honors in his final two years, with 949 receiving yards and nine touchdowns combined. But the Raiders have their two top tight ends cemented in Brock Bowers and Michael Mayer, along with some veterans and a project they like in Runyon. It’s unlikely Lauter gets anything more than a practice-squad spot.
Lafayette was an All-Sun Belt selection in 2025 as a versatile defensive back for the Trojans. He played a hybrid safety/linebacker role and possesses good run defense and ball skills. The Raiders needed safety help and added four defensive backs during the draft, leaving Lafayette with an uphill climb to hang around.
Pickett is a hulking offensive-line prospect who has the character the Raiders covet, serving as a team captain for the Blue Devils the last two seasons. He had his best collegiate season in 2025, earning All-ACC honors. The Raiders have a glut of interior offensive linemen with 10 guards and centers on their active roster, so Pickett will have to impress to stick with the team.
Linebacker is one of the Raiders’ weakest positions in terms of depth. The free-agent signings of Quay Walker and Nakobe Dean form a strong tandem, but none of their current backups saw much playing time in 2025. That opens an opportunity for an undrafted guy such as Thomas to impress. But transitioning to the NFL from FCS will be a challenge, even after making 120 tackles for the Black Bears last season.
Offord flashed strong ball skills during his lone season for the Owls, finishing second in Conference USA with 13 passes defensed. The Raiders made a point of adding more disruptors to their secondary through the draft, so Offord’s on-ball talents are likely what caught their attention. Continued production in that department could keep him on the practice squad.
The Raiders didn’t address wide receiver in the draft until the sixth-round selection of Malik Benson. However, they did bring in a trio of impressive UDFA wideouts. Rucker set all kinds of records for the Red Wolves and was productive in all five seasons he played in Jonesboro. Whether that success can continue against NFL competition will dictate his longevity in Las Vegas.
Clark had a strong finish to his college career, leading Missouri State to a winning record in its first FBS season while throwing for 3,244 yards and 28 touchdowns. The Raiders already have three quarterbacks they like in Mendoza, Kirk Cousins and Aidan O’Connell, though Clark could be a practice-squad candidate and potential emergency third quarterback if injuries occur or if O’Connell is moved.
Like Lafayette, Wall will enter camp behind a host of veterans as well as rookies Treydan Stukes and Dalton Johnson at safety. However, his skill set will allow him to play safety and nickel in Rob Leonard’s scheme. It wouldn’t be surprising to see him land on the practice squad.
While the Raiders have a lot of interior offensive linemen, their options on the outside are slim. There are four tackles on the roster, and Jatta makes five. He has multiple years of starting experience and is heralded for his run blocking, which the Raiders were awful at a season ago. He could be a practice-squad candidate and potential depth call-up.
Williams’ connection with Mendoza makes him an intriguing signing. He wasn’t the featured target during his lone season at Indiana, but they connected on some huge plays, including a touchdown in the College Football Playoff semifinals. Williams’ frame is ideal for a prototypical X receiver in the NFL and he could use built-in chemistry with his college quarterback to leave an impression.
Slone is touted for his high-effort play, a quality that will stand out to the coaching staff when he gets on the field. Dane Brugler, The Athletic ’s draft guru, says Slone has pass-rush skills worth developing as well, despite having just 1.5 sacks during his lone season for the Wolfpack. The Raiders have high-end pass rushers who they like, and they just added Keyron Crawford with a third-round pick. Slone’s motor could let him beat out some veterans for a depth spot.
The Raiders didn’t draft a defensive tackle until Brandon Cleveland in the seventh round, despite it being a perceived position of need. But they landed a strong UDFA in Smith. He’s a big nose tackle who is strong at the point of attack and quick to track down ball carriers, showcased by a career-high 40 tackles in 2025. Smith could compete with Cleveland for one of the final roster spots or land on the practice squad.
Roberts might have the best chance of the three UDFA receivers to crack the roster because of his skill set. What he lacks in speed he makes up for in size and craftiness. He’s capable of making the contested plays Mendoza excelled at in college, a quality no current Raider has proven to possess. Las Vegas could roster Roberts over a veteran to give the team a different type of receiver.
The backup job to Ashton Jeanty is up for grabs after the Raiders let Zamir White and Raheem Mostert walk. Fourth-round pick Mike Washington Jr. is the frontrunner for the role, but Hemby’s familiarity with Mendoza and his ability to execute zone and gap concepts could lead to success in camp. He should compete with Dylan Laube for the final running back spot on the roster.
Sorey will have the same opportunity as Thomas to take advantage of the team’s weak linebacker depth. But Sorey’s experience in Power 4 football, athleticism and motor should give him a leg up on his fellow UDFA. Sorey has some technique issues to clean up — missed tackles were prevalent in his college career — but as a former five-star recruit, he has the talent to play NFL football and could carve out a role with a strong offseason.
Matsuzawa should be in an open competition with Matt Gay after the Raiders let Daniel Carlson go this offseason. If the “Tokyo Toe” maintains the elite accuracy that made him a Lou Groza Award finalist last year, he could find himself the starting kicker — and the first Japanese-born athlete to ever play a snap in the NFL.
The only UDFA in a better position than Matsuzawa is the other specialist signee. Duzansky is heralded as the best long snapper in this class, being named a Patrick Mannelly Award finalist as a senior. The Raiders didn’t bring back Jacob Bobenmoyer and signed a possible replacement in Alex Ward, who was benched and cut by the Rams last season. Duzansky could have the upper hand on the starting job as he arrives in Las Vegas.

title: Execs unfiltered on every AFC team's draft: Are things finally looking up for Jets, Raiders? Mike Sando 35
summary:
Fernando Mendoza (right) is officially a Raider. Meanwhile David Bailey (center) and Kadyn Proctor headed draft classes praised by many around the league. Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; Photos: Ethan Miller / Getty Images, Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
After dissecting NFC teams’ drafts Thursday , we’re back with NFL executives’ insights into how all 16 AFC teams handled the annual player selection process.
Did the Buffalo Bills make wise use of all those picks (10) after trading
full_text:
Fernando Mendoza (right) is officially a Raider. Meanwhile David Bailey (center) and Kadyn Proctor headed draft classes praised by many around the league. Illustration: Demetrius Robinson / The Athletic; Photos: Ethan Miller / Getty Images, Emilee Chinn / Getty Images
After dissecting NFC teams’ drafts Thursday , we’re back with NFL executives’ insights into how all 16 AFC teams handled the annual player selection process.
Did the Buffalo Bills make wise use of all those picks (10) after trading down? Was the Cleveland Browns’ draft as good as the analysts suggested? Do the Houston Texans care what anyone thinks? Should the Indianapolis Colts regret the Sauce Gardner trade? Does anyone have anything good to say about Jaguars general manager James Gladstone? Is it really OK to feel good about the New York Jets?
Execs answer these and many more questions during my annual draft review.
For each team, we’ve included where it ranked in draft capital used (calculated using an NFL analytical model) and in Dane Brugler’s favorite classes , along with how many times it traded up or down during the draft (excluding deals that involved veteran players).
Draft capital rank: 11th | Brugler’s rank: 11th | Trades up/down: 1/0
The Ravens continued their recent trend of targeting less-premium positions in the first round, inviting an interesting philosophical discussion.
Guard Olaivavega Ioane (No. 14 this year) joins safety Malaki Starks (No. 27 in 2025), safety Kyle Hamilton (No. 14 in 2022) and center Tyler Linderbaum (No. 25 in 2022) among the recent Baltimore first-rounders fitting that mold.
All qualify as solid or even spectacular players.
Execs see Ioane as a high-odds prospect as well.
“Really good, good player — probably the best guard in the draft,” one said.
A thick, nasty mauler on track to be a long-term NFL starter.
The problem, if there is one, is that teams are generally less likely to re-sign players at these positions once their rookie contracts expire (Hamilton, the lone superstar among the group, did sign a four-year, $100.4 million deal before last season).
“The positional-value talk before the draft was interesting — teams said you can throw that out this year with the premium players playing non-premium positions,” another exec said. “(Sonny) Styles, (Caleb) Downs, (Jeremiyah) Love all fit that. Guards are expensive now, so it’s not as bad to pick up their options.
“Indy made it work with Quenton Nelson, and he was picked a lot higher (No. 6) than Ioane.”
Linderbaum’s case is instructive. He was everything the Ravens could have hoped, starting 66 of a possible 68 career games, earning three consecutive Pro Bowl honors and ranking fourth in Pro Football Focus’ grading for centers last season. But Baltimore declined his fifth-year option last spring because the value ($23.4 million) is tied to all offensive linemen (not centers, specifically). When his deal expired after four years, the Raiders signed him to a three-year, $81 million deal, resetting the market at the position by roughly 50 percent.
No one faults Baltimore for failing to meet that steep price, but if Ioane leaves in four years, no one should be shocked, either.
The void at center endures for Baltimore.
After using the first-round pick on Ioane and a second-rounder on an edge rusher (Zion Young), the Ravens watched two centers come off the board — Logan Jones to Chicago at No. 57, Jake Slaughter to the Chargers at No. 63 — before they were back on the clock at No. 80 and took receiver Ja’Kobi Lane.
Garrett Bradbury, acquired by Chicago from New England this offseason, would be a logical trade target if the Bears like what they see from Jones, the center they drafted in the second round. Bradbury played at NC State when current Ravens offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford coached the position for the Wolfpack.
“Baltimore is going to let everybody who can snap the ball try,” an exec said. “That would not be a bad trade. If I’m Chicago, I would not trade him until I know what I have with Logan Jones and know he is the guy.”
The Ravens doubled up on receiver and tight end in the third through fifth rounds.
“Ja’Kobi Lane is really talented — he has ability, but he’s really inconsistent,” an exec said of the Ravens’ third-round receiver. “(Matthew) Hibner is a good route-running tight end, has a little speed, catches it well, is perfect for them to develop. But he doesn’t have the body control that (Isaiah) Likely had.”
Draft capital rank: 25th | Brugler’s rank: 22nd | Trades up/down: 1/6
Execs admired the Bills’ ability to maneuver around the board while making a league-high seven in-draft trades, but reviews were mixed regarding the players Buffalo wound up selecting.
“Those picks you gain, whether it’s a third or fourth or something later, they were not going to net you any (good) players in this draft,” one exec said.
Time will tell on that front. The team drafted 10 players, tied for third-most in the league, and used its second-rounder to acquire receiver DJ Moore from Chicago.
“I do think there’s some element of regime change with (coach) Joe Brady and (GM) Brandon (Beane) wanting to make this his team and put in his stamp on it,” another exec said. “(Having) more picks probably helps do that. But again, this was a weird draft, in that it was terrible at the top and terrible at the bottom.”
“There was no sweet spot to accumulate picks,” this exec added. “I do not really begrudge anybody’s strategy in this draft, because I don’t know what you were supposed to do to be effective.”
The Bills traded down from 26 to 28, then to 31, then to 35, where they selected Clemson edge rusher T.J. Parker.
“The issue I have is, they took guys who have questionable play style,” a third exec said. “If you asked them what their identity is, they might say tough, physical, all these things. But you look at the guys they drafted, and it’s not that.”
“I was a big fan of Parker,” a different exec said. “Real young kid. Huge upside. The problem is, those Clemson defensive linemen, they just haven’t really developed, so there’s a little bit of a concern there.”
Still learning some moves, but offers playmaking potential against both run and pass.
Draft capital rank: 28th | Brugler’s rank: 24th | Trades up/down: 0/1
Execs applauded the Bengals’ decision to trade the 10th pick to the Giants for nose tackle Dexter Lawrence. They saw it as the surest way available for the Bengals to upgrade their defense and demonstrate to quarterback Joe Burrow that the team was serious, two huge priorities this offseason.
“This is like the NBA when you are trying to acquire guys to keep your star who is going to leave happy,” one exec said. “Is it expensive? Sure, but there is no price on keeping Burrow happy. Drafting Rueben Bain does not make Burrow happy.”
The Bengals also traded down with the Jets, who selected quarterback Cade Klubnik with Cincinnati’s pick in the fourth round. That deal helped the Bengals land receiver Colbie Young along with center Connor Lew.
“Young is legit — he’s big, and he’s got good hips and really good instincts for route running,” another exec said. “He is an outside receiver, though, so there is no one who can play the slot for them unless they put Ja’Marr Chase in there. It’s a helluva value pick. I just don’t know how you play all three at once.”
After effectively landing Lawrence with the 10th pick, the Bengals addressed defense with their own second- and third-round picks. They already added Boye Mafe, Bryan Cook and Jonathan Allen to deals totaling $45.9 million in average salary after letting edge rushers Trey Hendrickson and Joseph Ossai leave in free agency.
“Dexter Lawrence would be a top-five pick in this draft even at his age,” a third exec said. “There is no one like him in this draft. He can change their defense, coupled with what they did in free agency.”
